{{Short description|Machine learning algorithm}}
{{distinguish|Abbess|Leonard L. Abess}}

'''abess''' ('''Adaptive Best Subset Selection''', also '''ABESS''') is a [[machine learning]] method designed to address the problem of [[best subset selection]]. It aims to determine which features or variables are crucial for optimal model performance when provided with a dataset and a prediction task. '''abess''' was introduced by Zhu in 2020 <ref name = "zhu2020"/> and it dynamically selects the appropriate model size adaptively, eliminating the need for selecting regularization parameters.

'''abess''' is applicable in various statistical and machine learning tasks, including [[linear regression]], the [[Single-index model]], and other common predictive models.<ref name = "zhu2020"/><ref name = "tang2023"/> 
'''abess''' can also be applied in [[biostatistics]].<ref name = "kong2023"/><ref name = "reshetnikov2022"/><ref name = "liew2023"/><ref name = "wei2022"/>

== Basic Form ==

The basic form of '''abess''' <ref name = "zhu2020"/> is employed to address the optimal subset selection problem in [[linear regression|general linear regression]]. '''abess''' is an <math>l_0</math> method, it is characterized by its polynomial [[time complexity]] and the property of providing both [[Unbiased estimate|unbiased]] and [[Consistent estimator|consistent]] estimates.

In the context of linear regression, assuming we have knowledge of <math>n</math> independent samples <math>(x_i, y_i), i=1, \ldots, n</math>, where <math>x_i \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times 1}</math> and <math> y_i \in \mathbb{R} </math>, we define <math>X = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)^{\top}</math> and <math>y = (y_1, \ldots, y_n)^{\top}</math>. The following equation represents the general linear regression model:

<math>
    y = X\beta + \varepsilon.
</math>

To obtain appropriate parameters <math>\beta</math>, one can consider the [[loss function]] for linear regression:

<math>
    \mathcal{L}_n^{\text{LR}}(\beta; X, y) = \frac{1}{2n}\|y - X\beta\|_2^2.
</math>

In abess, the initial focus is on optimizing the loss function under the <math>l_0</math> constraint. That is, we consider the following problem:

<math>
    \min_{\beta \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times 1}} \mathcal{L}_n^{\text{LR}}(\beta; X, y), \text{ subject to } \|\beta\|_0 \leq s,
</math>

where <math>s</math> represents the desired size of the support set, and <math>\|\beta\|_0 = \sum_{i=1}^p \mathcal{I}_{(\beta_i \neq 0)}</math> is the <math>l_0</math> norm of the vector.

To address the [[optimization problem]] described above, '''abess''' iteratively exchanges an equal number of variables between the [[Support (mathematics)|active set]] and the inactive set. In each iteration, the concept of '''sacrifice''' is introduced as follows:

* For j in the active set (<math> j\in\hat{\mathcal A} </math>):
<math>
\xi_j = \mathcal L_n^{\text{LR}}\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\mathcal{A} \backslash\{j\}}\right) - \mathcal L_n^{\text{LR}}\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\mathcal{A}}\right) = \frac{\boldsymbol{X}_j^{\top} \boldsymbol{X}_j}{2 n}\left(\hat{\beta}_j\right)^2
</math>

* For j in the inactive set (<math> j\notin\hat{\mathcal A} </math>):
<math>
\xi_j = \mathcal L_n^{\text{LR}}\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\mathcal{A}}\right) - \mathcal L_n^{\text{LR}}\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\mathcal{A}}+\hat{\boldsymbol{t}}^{\{j\}}\right) = \frac{\boldsymbol{X}_j^{\top} \boldsymbol{X}_j}{2 n}\left(\frac{\hat{\mathrm{d}}_j}{\boldsymbol{X}_j^{\top} \boldsymbol{X}_j / n}\right)^2
</math>

Here are the key elements in the above equations:
* <math>\hat{\beta}^{\mathcal A}</math>: This represents the estimate of <math>\beta</math> obtained in the previous iteration.
* <math>\hat{\mathcal A}</math>: It denotes the estimated active set from the previous iteration.
* <math>\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\mathcal{A} \backslash\{j\}}</math>: This is a vector where the j-th element is set to 0, while the other elements are the same as <math>\hat{\beta}^{\mathcal A}</math>.
* <math>\hat{\boldsymbol{t}}^{\{j\}}=\arg \min _t \mathcal L_n^{\text{LR}}\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\mathcal{A}}+\boldsymbol{t}^{\{j\}}\right)</math>: Here, <math>t^{\{j\}}</math> represents a vector where all elements are 0 except the j-th element.
* <math>\hat{d}_j=\boldsymbol{X}_j^{\top}(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{X} \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) / n</math>: This is calculated based on the equation mentioned.

The iterative process involves exchanging variables, with the aim of minimizing the '''sacrifices''' in the active set while maximizing the '''sacrifices''' in the inactive set during each iteration. This approach allows '''abess''' to efficiently search for the optimal feature subset.

In '''abess''', select an appropriate <math>s_{\max}</math> and optimize the above problem for active sets size <math>s = 1, \ldots, s_{\max}</math> using the [[Information criterion (statistics)|information criterion]] <math> \text{GIC} = n \log \mathcal{L}_n^{\text{LR}} + s \log p \log \log n,</math> to adaptively choose the appropriate active set size <math>s</math> and obtain its corresponding '''abess''' estimator.

== Generalizations ==

The '''splicing algorithm''' in '''abess''' can be employed for subset selection in other models.

=== Distribution-Free Location-Scale Regression ===

In 2023, Siegfried extends '''abess''' to the case of Distribution-Free and Location-Scale.<ref name="siegfried2023"/> Specifically, it considers the optimization problem

<math>\max_{\boldsymbol{\vartheta} \in \mathbb{R}^P, \boldsymbol{\beta} \in \mathbb{R}^J, \boldsymbol{\gamma} \in \mathbb{R}^J} \sum_{i=1}^N \ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\vartheta}, \boldsymbol{x}_i^{\top} \boldsymbol{\beta},{\sqrt{\exp \left(\boldsymbol{x}_i^{\top} \boldsymbol{\gamma}\right)}}^{-1}\right),</math>

subject to <math>\left\|\left(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}^{\top}\right)^{\top}\right\|_0 \leq s,</math> where <math>\ell_i</math> is a loss function, <math>\boldsymbol{\vartheta}</math> is a parameter vector, <math>\boldsymbol{\beta}</math> and <math>\boldsymbol{\gamma}</math> are vectors, and <math>\boldsymbol{x}_i</math> is a data vector.

This approach, demonstrated across various applications, enables parsimonious regression modeling for arbitrary outcomes while maintaining interpretability through innovative subset selection procedures.

=== Groups Selection ===

In 2023, Zhang applied the '''splicing algorithm''' to group selection,<ref name = "zhang2023"/> optimizing the following model:

<math>
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta} \in \mathbb{R}^p} \mathcal L_n^{\text{LR}}(\beta;X,y) \text{ subject to } \sum_{j=1}^J I\left(\|\boldsymbol{\beta}_{G_j}\|_2 \neq 0\right) \leq s
</math>

Here are the symbols involved:

* <math>J</math>: Total number of feature groups, representing the existence of <math>J</math> non-overlapping feature groups in the dataset.
* <math>G_j</math>: [[Index set]] for the <math>j</math>-th feature group, where <math>j</math> ranges from 1 to <math>J</math>, representing the feature grouping structure in the data.
* <math>s</math>: Model size, a positive integer determined from the data, limiting the number of selected feature groups.

=== Regression with Corrupted Data ===

Zhang applied the '''splicing algorithm''' to handle corrupted data.<ref name = "zhang2024"/> Corrupted data refers to information that has been disrupted or contains errors during the data collection or recording process. This interference may include sensor inaccuracies, recording errors, communication issues, or other external disturbances, leading to inaccurate or distorted observations within the dataset.

=== Single Index Models ===

In 2023, Tang applied the '''splicing algorithm''' to optimal subset selection in the Single-index model.<ref name = "tang2023"/>

The form of the Single Index Model (SIM) is given by
<math>
y_i = g(\boldsymbol{b}^{\top} \boldsymbol{x}_i, e_i), \quad i = 1, \ldots, n,
</math>

where <math>\boldsymbol{b}</math> is the parameter vector,
<math>e_i</math> is the error term.

The corresponding loss function is defined as
<math>
l_n(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{r_i}{n} - \frac{1}{2} - \boldsymbol{x}_i^{\top} \boldsymbol{\beta}\right)^2,
</math>

where <math>\boldsymbol{r}</math> is the rank vector, <math>r_i</math> is the rank of <math>y_i</math> in <math>\boldsymbol{y}</math>.

The Estimation Problem addressed by this algorithm is
<math>
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} l_n(\boldsymbol{\beta}), \text { s.t. } \|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_0 \leq s.
</math>

=== Eographically Weighted Regression Model ===

In 2023, Wu <ref name="wu2023"/> applied the '''splicing algorithm''' to [[geographically weighted regression]] (GWR). GWR is a spatial analysis method, and Wu's research focuses on improving GWR performance in handling geographical data regression modeling. This is achieved through the application of an l0-norm variable adaptive selection method, which simultaneously performs model selection and coefficient optimization, enhancing the accuracy of regression modeling for geographic spatial data.

=== Distributed Systems ===

In 2023, Chen <ref name = "chen2023"/> introduced an innovative method addressing challenges in high-dimensional [[distributed systems]], proposing an efficient algorithm for '''abess'''. 

A distributed system is a computational model that distributes computing tasks across multiple independent nodes to achieve more efficient, reliable, and scalable [[data processing]]. In a distributed system, individual computing nodes can work simultaneously, collaboratively completing the overall tasks, thereby enhancing system performance and processing capabilities.

However, within distributed systems, there is a lack of efficient algorithms for optimal subset selection. To address this gap, Chen introduces a novel communication-efficient approach for handling optimal subset selection in distributed systems.

== Software Package ==

The '''abess''' library.<ref name = "zhu2022"/> (version 0.4.5) is an '''R package''' and '''python package''' based on C++ algorithms. It is [https://github.com/abess-team/abess open-source] on [[GitHub]]. The library can be used for optimal subset selection in linear regression, (multi-)classification, and censored-response modeling models. The abess package allows for parameters to be chosen in a grouped format. Information and tutorials are available on the abess homepage.<ref name = "abess"/>

== Application ==

'''abess''' can be applied in biostatistics, such as assessing the robust severity of [[COVID-19]] patients,<ref name = "kong2023"/> conducting [[antibiotic resistance]] in [[Mycobacterium tuberculosis]],<ref name = "reshetnikov2022"/> exploring prognostic factors in [[neck pain]],<ref name = "liew2023"/> and developing prediction models for severe pain in patients after [[percutaneous nephrolithotomy]].<ref name = "wei2022"/> '''abess''' can also be applied to gene selection.<ref name = "miao2022"/> In the field of data-driven [[partial differential equation]] (PDE) discovery, Thanasutives <ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Thanasutives |first1=Pongpisit |last2=Morita |first2=Takashi |last3=Numao |first3=Masayuki |last4=Fukui |first4=Ken-ichi |date=2023-02-01 |title=Noise-aware physics-informed machine learning for robust PDE discovery |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/2632-2153/acb1f0 |journal=Machine Learning: Science and Technology |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=015009 |doi=10.1088/2632-2153/acb1f0 |issn=2632-2153|arxiv=2206.12901 |bibcode=2023MLS&T...4a5009T }}</ref> applied '''abess''' to automatically identify parsimonious governing PDEs.
